To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the speech error pattern for the genetically transmitted subtype of childhood speech delay of unknown cause is characterized by a higher proportion of relative omissions and a lower proportion of relative distortions, particularly of sibilant frictions, compared with other proposed subtypes, with the latter being associated with a higher proportion of backed /S/ distortions.

children with speech delay who have 2 or more nuclear family members who currently and/or previously had speech-language disorder (a) have a higher proportion of relative consonant omission errors, particularly on the Late-9 consonants, (b) have a lower proportion of relative consonantal distortion errors, particularly on fricatives, and (c) have a lower relative proportion of backed /S/ distortions.

children with speech delay with 2+ affected nuclear family members (possibly higher genetic load) had (a higher proportion of relative omissions on the Late- 8 consonants; and (b) a lower proportion of relative distortions, particularly on the fricative /s/, and (c) fewer backed /s/ errors.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the hypothesis that the commonest subtype of SSD is genetically transmitted.
the identification of a speech error pattern for a proposed genetically transmitted subtype of SSD.
the development and validation of a set of diagnostic and phenotype markers that will be used to identify children with speech delay that is genetically transmitted.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
this study provides evidence that children with genetically transmitted speech delay have different error patterns than children who may not have a genetic load for SSD.
the speech error pattern of the proposed subtype of SSD of unknown genetic origin with higher genetic load for speech disorders is consistent with a cognitive-linguistics processing deficit.
the speech error patterns of the proposed speech delay-genetic subtype of SSD are consistent with the hypothesis of a genetically transmitted subtype of SSD of currently unknown origin.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the proposed speech delay-genetic subtype is characterized by a relative reduction in speech error patterns that reflect phonetic processing deficits, and a relative increase in error patterns that reflect lexical processing deficits.

the proposed subtype of SSD with a genetic etiology has a distinctive pattern of speech error types that can be identified by speech and language professionals and that may be useful for research and clinical purposes.

the proposed speech delay-genetic subtype is characterized by a specific error pattern that is consistent with the cognitive and linguistic deficits that are known to be associated with genetic disorders of language.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the error pattern for this subtype of speech delay of unknown etiology can be reliably differentiated from the error pattern for other subtypes, including those with possible environmental origins.
a set of phenotype markers for this proposed etiological subgroup of speech delay may be possible to develop.
the proposed genetic etiology of a substantial proportion of SSD is supported by converging evidence.
